topics: Matrix powers, Cayley–Hamilton & systems of ODEs

body.en: Under a general linear transformation, vectors typically experience both stretching and rotation. An eigenvector identifies an invariant direction that is purely scaled by a scalar factor known as the eigenvalue. Spectral theory decouples coupled linear systems, enabling explicit computation of matrix powers, Markov processes, and systems of linear differential equations.
body.ar: Under a general linear transformation, المتجهات typically experience both stretching and rotation. An eigenvector identifies an invariant direction that is purely scaled by a scalar factor known as the eigenvalue. Spectral theory decouples coupled linear systems, enabling explicit computation of المصفوفة powers, Markov processes, and systems of linear differential المعادلات.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, Eigenspaces & Characteristic Equations

body.en: Let \( A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \). A non-zero vector \( \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n \) is an eigenvector of \( A \) corresponding to eigenvalue \( \lambda \in \mathbb{C} \) if: \[ A\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} \quad (\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}). \]
body.ar: Let \( A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \). A non-zero المتجه \( \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n \) is an eigenvector of \( A \) corresponding to eigenvalue \( \lambda \in \mathbb{C} \) if: \[ A\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} \quad (\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}). \]

label.ar: ● تعريف 6.1 — Eigenspaces & The Characteristic كثيرة الحدود

body.en:
1. Eigenspace: For a given eigenvalue \( \lambda \), the set of all eigenvectors along with the zero vector forms a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^n \), the eigenspace \( E_\lambda \): \[ E_\lambda = \operatorname{Null}(A - \lambda I) = \{ \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n : (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \}. \]

2. The Characteristic Equation: The homogeneous system \( (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \) has a non-trivial solution \( \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0} \) if and only if \( A - \lambda I \) is singular (non-invertible): \[ p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = 0. \] Expanding the determinant yields a degree-\( n \) polynomial in \( \lambda \), the characteristic polynomial.

3. Trace & Determinant Invariants: If \( \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n \) are the eigenvalues of \( A \) counted with multiplicity: \[ \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ii}, \qquad \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \det(A). \]
body.ar:
1. Eigenspace: For a المعطيات eigenvalue \( \lambda \), the set of all المتجهات الذاتية along with the zero المتجه forms a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^n \), the eigenspace \( E_\lambda \): \[ E_\lambda = \operatorname{Null}(A - \lambda I) = \{ \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n : (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \}. \]

2. The Characteristic المعادلة: The homogeneous system \( (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \) has a non-trivial الحل \( \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0} \) if and only if \( A - \lambda I \) is singular (non-invertible): \[ p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = 0. \] Expanding the المحدد yields a degree-\( n \) كثيرة الحدود in \( \lambda \), the characteristic polynomial.

3. Trace & المحدد Invariants: If \( \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n \) are the القيم الذاتية of \( A \) counted with multiplicity: \[ \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ii}, \qquad \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \det(A). \]

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & Diagonalization)
label.ar: ◆ لماذا تعمل هذه الطريقة رياضياً — First-Principles اشتقاق (القيم الذاتية, المتجهات الذاتية & Diagonalization)

body.en:
Why Orthogonal Projection & Eigenvalue Characteristic Equations Work: Decompose \(\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\) where \(\mathbf{w} \perp \mathbf{v}\). Taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{v}\) uses \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) to isolate \(c\):

\[ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + 0 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2} \]

For eigenvalues, \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) is equivalent to \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\). A homogeneous linear system has a non-trivial nullspace vector \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) if and only if the matrix \(A - \lambda I\) is singular, yielding the characteristic polynomial \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\).
body.ar:
Why Orthogonal Projection & Eigenvalue Characteristic المعادلات Work: Decompose \(\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\) حيث \(\mathbf{w} \perp \mathbf{v}\). Taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{v}\) uses \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) to isolate \(c\):

\[ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + 0 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2} \]

For القيم الذاتية, \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) is equivalent to \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\). A homogeneous linear system has a non-trivial nullspace المتجه \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) if and only if the المصفوفة \(A - \lambda I\) is singular, yielding the characteristic كثيرة الحدود \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\).

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Worked Example · Computing Eigenvalues, Eigenspaces & Invariant Checks
label.ar: Level 1 (Foundations) — مثال محلول · Computing القيم الذاتية, Eigenspaces & Invariant Checks

body.en:
Problem: Find the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenspace bases for \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), and verify the trace and determinant relations.

Step 1 · Solve Characteristic Equation: \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = \begin{vmatrix} 4 - \lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = (4 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda) - (1)(2) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 12 - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0. \] Factoring: \[ (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2) = 0 \implies \mathbf{\lambda_1 = 5, \quad \lambda_2 = 2}. \]

Step 2 · Verify Invariants:
• \( \operatorname{tr}(A) = 4 + 3 = 7 \), and \( \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 5 + 2 = 7 \). ✓
• \( \det(A) = (4)(3) - (1)(2) = 10 \), and \( \lambda_1 \lambda_2 = (5)(2) = 10 \). ✓

Step 3 · Eigenspace \( E_5 \) (\( \lambda = 5 \)): \[ A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_2 \leftarrow R_2 + 2R_1} \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies -v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}}. \]

Step 4 · Eigenspace \( E_2 \) (\( \lambda = 2 \)): \[ A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies 2v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}}. \]
body.ar:
Problem: أوجد القيم الذاتية and corresponding eigenspace bases for \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), and verify the trace and المحدد relations.

Step 1 · Solve Characteristic المعادلة: \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = \begin{vmatrix} 4 - \lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = (4 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda) - (1)(2) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 12 - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0. \] Factoring: \[ (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2) = 0 \implies \mathbf{\lambda_1 = 5, \quad \lambda_2 = 2}. \]

Step 2 · Verify Invariants:
• \( \operatorname{tr}(A) = 4 + 3 = 7 \), and \( \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 5 + 2 = 7 \). ✓
• \( \det(A) = (4)(3) - (1)(2) = 10 \), and \( \lambda_1 \lambda_2 = (5)(2) = 10 \). ✓

Step 3 · Eigenspace \( E_5 \) (\( \lambda = 5 \)): \[ A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_2 \leftarrow R_2 + 2R_1} \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies -v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}}. \]

Step 4 · Eigenspace \( E_2 \) (\( \lambda = 2 \)): \[ A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \implies 2v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}}. \]

label.ar: مثال محلول \(B\) — القيم الذاتية, المتجهات الذاتية & Diagonalization (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): Consider a linear transformation represented by the diagonal matrix \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \). If \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \) is an eigenvector of \( A \), what is the corresponding eigenvalue?

Step-by-Step Solution: Multiplying \( A \) by \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \) gives: \[ A\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 3\mathbf{v}. \] Thus, the corresponding eigenvalue is \( \lambda = 3 \).
body.ar:
Problem (Medium): Consider a linear transformation represented by the diagonal المصفوفة \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \). If \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \) is an eigenvector of \( A \), what is the corresponding eigenvalue?

Step-by-Step الحل: Multiplying \( A \) by \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \) gives: \[ A\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 3\mathbf{v}. \] وعليه, the corresponding eigenvalue is \( \lambda = 3 \).

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Find the eigenvalues of the upper-triangular matrix: \[ T = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. \]
question.ar:
Level 1 · Foundations

أوجد القيم الذاتية لـ the upper-triangular matrix: \[ T = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. \]

solution.en: The characteristic matrix is: \[ T - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix} 6 - \lambda & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 - \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 - \lambda \end{pmatrix}. \] Since \( T - \lambda I \) is upper-triangular, its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries: \[ \det(T - \lambda I) = (6 - \lambda)(-3 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) = 0. \] Thus the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries themselves: \[ \mathbf{\lambda_1 = 6, \quad \lambda_2 = -3, \quad \lambda_3 = 4}. \]
solution.ar:

The characteristic matrix is: \[ T - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix} 6 - \lambda & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 - \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 - \lambda \end{pmatrix}. \] Since \( T - \lambda I \) is upper-triangular, its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries: \[ \det(T - \lambda I) = (6 - \lambda)(-3 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) = 0. \] Thus the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries themselves: \[ \mathbf{\lambda_1 = 6, \quad \lambda_2 = -3, \quad \lambda_3 = 4}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Linear Independence of Eigenvectors & Matrix Diagonalization

body.en: When a matrix has a full set of linearly independent eigenvectors, it can be factored into a product \( A = P D P^{-1} \) where \( D \) is diagonal. This diagonal representation decouples the action of \( A \) into independent 1D scalings along the eigenvector coordinate axes.
body.ar: عندما a المصفوفة has a full set of linearly independent المتجهات الذاتية, it can be factored into a product \( A = P D P^{-1} \) حيث \( D \) is diagonal. This diagonal representation decouples the action of \( A \) into independent 1D scalings along the eigenvector الإحداثي axes.

label.en: ● Theorem 6.1 & Analytical Proof · Independence of Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues
label.ar: ● مبرهنة 6.1 & Analytical برهان · Independence of المتجهات الذاتية for Distinct القيم الذاتية

body.en:
Theorem: Let \( \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k \) be eigenvectors of \( A \) corresponding to mutually distinct eigenvalues \( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_k \) (i.e. \( \lambda_i eq \lambda_j \) for \( i eq j \)). Then the set \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k \} \) is linearly independent.

Proof by Induction:
• Base Case (\( k = 1 \)): \( \mathbf{v}_1 eq \mathbf{0} \) by definition of an eigenvector, so \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1 \} \) is linearly independent.
• Inductive Step: Assume the statement holds for \( k - 1 \) eigenvectors. Suppose: \[ c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 1)} \] Multiply both sides by \( \lambda_k \): \[ c_1 \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 2)} \] Apply the matrix \( A \) to Equation 1, using \( A\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i \): \[ c_1 \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 3)} \] Subtract Equation 2 from Equation 3: \[ c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_{k-1}(\lambda_{k-1} - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}. \] By the inductive hypothesis, \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{k-1} \} \) is linearly independent, so each coefficient must be zero: \[ c_i(\lambda_i - \lambda_k) = 0 \quad ext{for } i = 1, \dots, k - 1. \] Because all eigenvalues are distinct, \( \lambda_i - \lambda_k eq 0 \), forcing \( c_i = 0 \) for all \( i = 1, \dots, k - 1 \). Substituting these zeros back into Equation 1 gives \( c_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0} \), which forces \( c_k = 0 \) since \( \mathbf{v}_k eq \mathbf{0} \).
Therefore, all \( c_i = 0 \), proving linear independence. \( lacksquare\)
body.ar:
Theorem: Let \( \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k \) be المتجهات الذاتية of \( A \) corresponding to mutually distinct القيم الذاتية \( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_k \) (i.e. \( \lambda_i eq \lambda_j \) for \( i eq j \)). Then the set \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k \} \) is linearly independent.

Proof by Induction:
• Base Case (\( k = 1 \)): \( \mathbf{v}_1 eq \mathbf{0} \) by definition of an eigenvector, so \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1 \} \) is linearly independent.
• Inductive Step: Assume the statement holds for \( k - 1 \) المتجهات الذاتية. Suppose: \[ c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 1)} \] Multiply both sides by \( \lambda_k \): \[ c_1 \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 2)} \] Apply the المصفوفة \( A \) to المعادلة 1, using \( A\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i \): \[ c_1 \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}. \quad ext{(Equation 3)} \] Subtract المعادلة 2 from المعادلة 3: \[ c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2(\lambda_2 - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_{k-1}(\lambda_{k-1} - \lambda_k)\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}. \] By the inductive hypothesis, \( \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{k-1} \} \) is linearly independent, so each المعامل must be zero: \[ c_i(\lambda_i - \lambda_k) = 0 \quad ext{for } i = 1, \dots, k - 1. \] Because all القيم الذاتية are distinct, \( \lambda_i - \lambda_k eq 0 \), forcing \( c_i = 0 \) for all \( i = 1, \dots, k - 1 \). Substituting these zeros back into المعادلة 1 gives \( c_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0} \), which forces \( c_k = 0 \) since \( \mathbf{v}_k eq \mathbf{0} \).
Therefore, all \( c_i = 0 \), proving linear independence. \( lacksquare\)

body.en:
An \( n \times n \) matrix \( A \) is diagonalizable (there exists invertible \( P \) and diagonal \( D \) such that \( A = P D P^{-1} \)) if and only if \( A \) has \( n \) linearly independent eigenvectors.

In this case: \[ P = [\mathbf{v}_1 \; \mathbf{v}_2 \; \dots \; \mathbf{v}_n], \qquad D = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & \lambda_n \end{pmatrix}, \] where column \( j \) of \( P \) is an eigenvector corresponding to the diagonal entry \( \lambda_j \) in \( D \).

Corollaries:
• If \( A \) has \( n \) distinct eigenvalues, \( A \) is automatically diagonalizable.
• Powers of \( A \): For any integer \( k \ge 1 \), \[ A^k = P D^k P^{-1} = P \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^k & & 0 \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & \lambda_n^k \end{pmatrix} P^{-1}. \]
body.ar:
An \( n \times n \) المصفوفة \( A \) is diagonalizable (there exists invertible \( P \) and diagonal \( D \) such that \( A = P D P^{-1} \)) if and only if \( A \) has \( n \) linearly independent المتجهات الذاتية.

In this case: \[ P = [\mathbf{v}_1 \; \mathbf{v}_2 \; \dots \; \mathbf{v}_n], \qquad D = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & \lambda_n \end{pmatrix}, \] حيث column \( j \) of \( P \) is an eigenvector corresponding to the diagonal entry \( \lambda_j \) in \( D \).

Corollaries:
• If \( A \) has \( n \) distinct القيم الذاتية, \( A \) is automatically diagonalizable.
• Powers of \( A \): For any integer \( k \ge 1 \), \[ A^k = P D^k P^{-1} = P \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^k & & 0 \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & \lambda_n^k \end{pmatrix} P^{-1}. \]

body.en:
Problem: Compute \( A^{10} \) for \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) using diagonalization.

Step 1 · Find Eigenvalues: \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)^2 - 9 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 8 = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda + 2) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 4, \quad \lambda_2 = -2. \]

Step 2 · Find Eigenvectors:
• For \( \lambda = 4 \): \( A - 4I = \begin{pmatrix} -3 & 3 \\ 3 & -3 \end{pmatrix} \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).
• For \( \lambda = -2 \): \( A + 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 3 · Construct \( P \), \( D \), and \( P^{-1} \): \[ P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. \] \[ \det(P) = 1(1) - (-1)(1) = 2 \implies P^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 4 · Compute \( A^{10} = P D^{10} P^{-1} \): \[ D^{10} = \begin{pmatrix} 4^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & (-2)^{10} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1048576 & 0 \\ 0 & 1024 \end{pmatrix}. \] \[ A^{10} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 4^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 2^{10} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 4^{10} & -2^{10} \\ 4^{10} & 2^{10} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \] \[ A^{10} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 4^{10} + 2^{10} & 4^{10} - 2^{10} \\ 4^{10} - 2^{10} & 4^{10} + 2^{10} \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 524800 & 523776 \\ 523776 & 524800 \end{pmatrix}}. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Explain why the matrix \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) is not diagonalizable.
question.ar:
حل المسألة التالية في (Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & Diagonalization): Level 2 · Medium

Explain why the matrix \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) is not diagonalizable.

solution.en:
Step 1 · Algebraic Multiplicity: \( A \) is upper-triangular, so its characteristic polynomial is \( p(\lambda) = (3 - \lambda)^2 = 0 \). The only eigenvalue is \( \lambda = 3 \) with algebraic multiplicity \( m_a(3) = 2 \).

Step 2 · Geometric Multiplicity: Compute the eigenspace \( E_3 = \operatorname{Null}(A - 3I) \): \[ A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \] This matrix has pivot in column 2, with only one free variable \( x_1 = t \). The eigenvectors are \( \mathbf{v} = t \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \), so \( \dim(E_3) = 1 \).

Conclusion: Since the geometric multiplicity \( m_g(3) = 1 \) is strictly less than the algebraic multiplicity \( m_a(3) = 2 \), \( A \) fails to possess 2 linearly independent eigenvectors. Therefore, \( A \) is defective and NOT diagonalizable.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor — The Cayley–Hamilton Theorem & Matrix Differential Equations

body.en: The Cayley–Hamilton Theorem asserts that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, providing a powerful analytic tool for computing inverse matrices and powers. Furthermore, spectral theory solves systems of first-order linear differential equations \( \mathbf{x}'(t) = A\mathbf{x}(t) \) via the matrix exponential.
body.ar: The Cayley–Hamilton مبرهنة asserts that every square المصفوفة satisfies its own characteristic المعادلة, providing a powerful analytic tool for computing inverse المصفوفات and powers. Furthermore, spectral theory solves systems of first-order linear differential المعادلات \( \mathbf{x}'(t) = A\mathbf{x}(t) \) via the المصفوفة exponential.

body.en:
Theorem (Cayley–Hamilton): Let \( A \) be an \( n \times n \) matrix with characteristic polynomial \( p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = (-1)^n \lambda^n + c_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + c_1 \lambda + c_0 \). Then substituting \( A \) into its own polynomial yields the zero matrix: \[ p(A) = (-1)^n A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \dots + c_1 A + c_0 I = 0. \]

Proof via Adjugate Matrix: Recall from Theorem 4.2 that for any square matrix, \( M \operatorname{adj}(M) = \det(M) I \). Setting \( M = A - \lambda I \): \[ (A - \lambda I) \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I. \] The entries of \( \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) \) are cofactors of \( A - \lambda I \), which are polynomials in \( \lambda \) of degree at most \( n - 1 \). Therefore, \( \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) \) can be expanded as a matrix polynomial: \[ \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) = B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + B_{n-2} \lambda^{n-2} + \dots + B_1 \lambda + B_0, \] where each \( B_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \). Substituting into the adjugate identity: \[ (A - \lambda I)(B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + B_0) = (c_n \lambda^n + c_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + c_0) I. \] Expanding and equating coefficients of \( \lambda^k \) yields a telescoping sequence of matrix equations. Pre-multiplying the \( k \)-th equation by \( A^k \) and summing all equations eliminates all terms on the left side, yielding \( 0 = p(A) \). \(\blacksquare\)
body.ar:
Theorem (Cayley–Hamilton): Let \( A \) be an \( n \times n \) المصفوفة with characteristic كثيرة الحدود \( p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = (-1)^n \lambda^n + c_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + c_1 \lambda + c_0 \). Then substituting \( A \) into its own كثيرة الحدود yields the zero المصفوفة: \[ p(A) = (-1)^n A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \dots + c_1 A + c_0 I = 0. \]

Proof via Adjugate المصفوفة: Recall from مبرهنة 4.2 that for any square المصفوفة, \( M \operatorname{adj}(M) = \det(M) I \). Setting \( M = A - \lambda I \): \[ (A - \lambda I) \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I. \] The entries of \( \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) \) are cofactors of \( A - \lambda I \), which are polynomials in \( \lambda \) of degree at most \( n - 1 \). وبالتالي, \( \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) \) can be expanded as a المصفوفة كثيرة الحدود: \[ \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I) = B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + B_{n-2} \lambda^{n-2} + \dots + B_1 \lambda + B_0, \] حيث each \( B_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \). Substituting into the adjugate المتطابقة: \[ (A - \lambda I)(B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + B_0) = (c_n \lambda^n + c_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + c_0) I. \] Expanding and equating المعاملات of \( \lambda^k \) yields a telescoping المتتالية of المصفوفة المعادلات. Pre-multiplying the \( k \)-th المعادلة by \( A^k \) and summing all المعادلات eliminates all terms on the left side, yielding \( 0 = p(A) \). \(\blacksquare\)

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & University Pitfalls · Eigenvalues & Diagonalization
label.ar: ⚠️ أخطاء شائعة ومصائد جامعية · القيم الذاتية & Diagonalization

body.en:
1. Row Operations Alter Eigenvalues: Performing elementary row operations \( A \to R \) preserves row space and null space, but completely destroys eigenvalues: \( \det(A - \lambda I) \neq \det(R - \lambda I) \). Never row reduce \( A \) prior to setting up \( \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \)!
  2. Defective Matrices: Having repeated eigenvalues (\( m_a(\lambda) \ge 2 \)) does NOT automatically mean the matrix is not diagonalizable. For example, \( I_2 \) has \( \lambda = 1 \) with multiplicity 2, but \( E_1 = \mathbb{R}^2 \) has dimension 2, so \( I_2 \) is diagonalizable. A matrix is non-diagonalizable only when \( m_g(\lambda) < m_a(\lambda) \) for some eigenvalue.
  3. Complex Eigenvalues for Real Matrices: A real matrix can have complex conjugate eigenvalues \( a \pm bi \) representing rotation-dilations. A real matrix with complex eigenvalues is not diagonalizable over \( \mathbb{R} \) (though it is diagonalizable over \( \mathbb{C} \)).
body.ar:
1. Row Operations Alter القيم الذاتية: Performing elementary row operations \( A \to R \) preserves row space and null space, but completely destroys eigenvalues: \( \det(A - \lambda I) \neq \det(R - \lambda I) \). Never row reduce \( A \) prior to setting up \( \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \)!
  2. Defective المصفوفات: Having repeated القيم الذاتية (\( m_a(\lambda) \ge 2 \)) does NOT automatically mean the المصفوفة is not diagonalizable. For example, \( I_2 \) has \( \lambda = 1 \) with multiplicity 2, but \( E_1 = \mathbb{R}^2 \) has dimension 2, so \( I_2 \) is diagonalizable. A المصفوفة is non-diagonalizable only عندما \( m_g(\lambda) < m_a(\lambda) \) for some eigenvalue.
  3. Complex القيم الذاتية for Real المصفوفات: A real المصفوفة can have complex conjugate القيم الذاتية \( a \pm bi \) representing rotation-dilations. A real المصفوفة with complex القيم الذاتية is not diagonalizable over \( \mathbb{R} \) (though it is diagonalizable over \( \mathbb{C} \)).

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced) — Worked Example · Systems of Differential Equations via Diagonalization
label.ar: Level 3 (Advanced) — مثال محلول · Systems of Differential المعادلات via Diagonalization

body.en:
Problem: Solve the initial value problem for the coupled linear ODE system: \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \qquad \mathbf{x}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 1 · Diagonalize Coefficient Matrix \( A \): \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 3, \; \lambda_2 = -1. \] • For \( \lambda_1 = 3 \): \( A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).
• For \( \lambda_2 = -1 \): \( A + I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2 · Decouple via Coordinate Change \( \mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y} \):
Since \( A = P D P^{-1} \), \( \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x} \implies P\mathbf{y}' = P D \mathbf{y} \implies \mathbf{y}' = D\mathbf{y} \).
The decoupled solutions are \( y_1(t) = c_1 e^{3t} \) and \( y_2(t) = c_2 e^{-t} \). Therefore: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{3t} \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{-t} \mathbf{v}_2 = c_1 e^{3t} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + c_2 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 3 · Apply Initial Condition \( \mathbf{x}(0) = (5, 1)^T \): \[ c_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + c_2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{aligned} c_1 + c_2 &= 5 \\ c_1 - c_2 &= 1 \end{aligned} \implies c_1 = 3, \; c_2 = 2. \] \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{3e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + 2e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3e^{3t} + 2e^{-t} \\ 3e^{3t} - 2e^{-t} \end{pmatrix}}. \]

Step 1 · Diagonalize المعامل المصفوفة \( A \): \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 3, \; \lambda_2 = -1. \] • For \( \lambda_1 = 3 \): \( A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2 · Decouple via الإحداثي Change \( \mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y} \):

Step 3 · Apply Initial Condition \( \mathbf{x}(0) = (5, 1)^T \): \[ c_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + c_2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{aligned} c_1 + c_2 &= 5 \\ c_1 - c_2 &= 1 \end{aligned} \implies c_1 = 3, \; c_2 = 2. \] \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{3e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + 2e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3e^{3t} + 2e^{-t} \\ 3e^{3t} - 2e^{-t} \end{pmatrix}}. \]

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor

Let \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \). Using the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem, express \( A^4 \) and \( A^{-1} \) as linear combinations \( c_1 A + c_0 I \).
question.ar:
Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor

ليكن \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \). باستخدام Cayley–Hamilton Theorem, express \( A^4 \) and \( A^{-1} \) as linear combinations \( c_1 A + c_0 I \).

solution.en:
Step 1 · Find Characteristic Polynomial: \[ p(\lambda) = (2 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda) - 0 = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6. \]

Step 2 · Apply Cayley–Hamilton: \( A^2 - 5A + 6I = 0 \):
From this: \( A^2 = 5A - 6I \). Multiply by \( A \): \[ A^3 = 5A^2 - 6A = 5(5A - 6I) - 6A = 25A - 30I - 6A = 19A - 30I. \] Multiply by \( A \) again: \[ A^4 = 19A^2 - 30A = 19(5A - 6I) - 30A = 95A - 114I - 30A = \mathbf{65A - 114I}. \]

Step 3 · Express \( A^{-1} \): Multiply \( A^2 - 5A + 6I = 0 \) by \( A^{-1} \): \[ A - 5I + 6A^{-1} = 0 \implies 6A^{-1} = 5I - A \implies \mathbf{A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{6}A + \frac{5}{6}I}. \]
solution.ar:

From this: \( A^2 = 5A - 6I \). Multiply by \( A \): \[ A^3 = 5A^2 - 6A = 5(5A - 6I) - 6A = 25A - 30I - 6A = 19A - 30I. \] Multiply by \( A \) again: \[ A^4 = 19A^2 - 30A = 19(5A - 6I) - 30A = 95A - 114I - 30A = \mathbf{65A - 114I}. \]

Step 3 · Express \( A^{-1} \): Multiply \( A^2 - 5A + 6I = 0 \) by \( A^{-1} \): \[ A - 5I + 6A^{-1} = 0 \implies 6A^{-1} = 5I - A \implies \mathbf{A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{6}A + \frac{5}{6}I}. \]
